summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.
title: Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models

summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.
title: A COMSOL framework for predicting hydrogen embrittlement -- Part I: coupled hydrogen transport

summary: We study the performance of sequential contention resolution and matching algorithms on random graphs with vanishing edge probabilities. When the edges of the graph are processed in an adversarially-chosen order, we derive a new OCRS that is $0.382$-selectable, attaining the "independence benchmark" from the literature under the vanishing edge probabilities assumption. Complementary to this positive result, we show that no OCRS can be more than $0.390$-selectable, significantly improving upon the upper bound of $0.428$ from the literature. We also derive negative results that are specialized to bipartite graphs or subfamilies of OCRSs. Meanwhile, when the edges of the graph are processed in a uniformly random order, we show that the simple greedy contention resolution scheme which accepts all active and feasible edges is $1/2$-selectable. This result is tight due to a known upper bound. We then show that when the algorithm can choose the processing order, a slight tweak to the random order---give each vertex a random priority and process edges in lexicographic order---results in a strictly better contention resolution scheme that is $1-\ln(2-1/e)\approx0.510$-selectable. Moreover, we show that this bound is tight over any sequential contention resolution scheme, even one which may adaptively choose the order in which it processes edges. This provides a separation from the $0.544$ upper bound for offline contention resolution implied by the classic result of Karp and Sipser. Our positive results also apply to online matching on $1$-uniform random graphs with vanishing (non-identical) edge probabilities, extending and unifying some results from the random graphs literature.
title: Online Matching and Contention Resolution for Edge Arrivals with Vanishing Probabilities

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. We compare the approach against state-of-the-art techniques, over polynomial and non-polynomial dynamical models: the outcomes show that we can synthesise sound BCs up to two orders of magnitude faster, with in particular a stark speedup on the verification engine (up to five orders less), whilst needing a far smaller data set (up to three orders less) for the learning part. Beyond improvements over the state of the art, we further challenge the new approach on a hybrid dynamical model and on larger-dimensional models, and showcase the numerical robustness of our algorithms and codebase.

summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. Leadership measurement should focus on accepted outcome rate, cost per accepted outcome, realised business value, consequential errors, latency distribution, policy compliance, escalation and rework, and model substitution readiness. The central argument is that enterprise advantage will come from disciplined allocation of intelligence rather than maximising model capability or model count. The appropriate question is which intelligence should handle each workload, under what authority, and at what verified cost of successful execution. The AI Workload Classification framework, Model Routing Matrix, Capability-Cost Frontier, Model Escalation Ladder, Minimum Sufficient Intelligence principle and Cost per Accepted Outcome framework are author-developed analytical constructs. No human treatment, needle insertion, device authorization, quantum advantage or clinical recovery is shown. Traditional acupuncture, Daoism, yin–yang, qi and meridian philosophy are treated as cultural and interpretative traditions, not as independently demonstrated new SI physical fields. Five official fourth-family flagships F016 | Electrical–Mechanical Signal Fusion in Acupuncture at the Limit / 針灸電訊號與機械訊號融合極限 F017 | Thermal Signal–Skin Impedance Coupling in Acupuncture at the Limit / 針灸熱訊號與皮膚阻抗耦合極限 F018 | Ultrasound–Electrophysiology Fusion for Acupuncture Localization at the Limit / 針灸超音波與電生理定位融合極限 F019 | Multimodal Signal Synchronization and Calibration at the Limit / 針灸多模態訊號同步校準極限 F020 | Multimodal Acupuncture State Reconstruction at the Limit / 針灸多模態狀態重建極限 The dual-book architecture F016 — Electrical–mechanical signal fusion Core three-coupling: differential electrical sensing / calibrated force-strain reference / clock-independent multimodal correspondence. Physical bench: inert conductive-elastomer phantom with isolated microvolt source, load-cell reference and optically tracked deformation. Strong baseline: best single calibrated electrical or mechanical sensor at matched acquisition, tuning, energy and calibration budgets. Primary endpoint: electrical-mechanical cross-sensor onset skew [ms]. Critical rival: cable microphonics, shared chassis vibration, electrode polarization, common reference timing and force-induced contact artefacts. Noncompensable stop: lost galvanic isolation, unmatched hardware timestamps, sensor saturation, or unsupported inference about biological meridians. Five evidence channels must never be reduced to a flattering fusion score. Force and microvolts, heat and impedance, acoustic fiducials, independent clock witnesses and inferred latent states are separate objects with different scales. A joint model cannot substitute for physical calibration or the best single-sensor comparison. The falsifiable claim is transferred from one laboratory to another only after physical scale, reference identity, data selection, external event time, software version and valid authorization are declared. The source lineage may motivate a new hypothesis, but the assertion must survive a separate experiment. F017 — Thermal–impedance coupling Core three-coupling: independent thermography / frequency-resolved impedance spectroscopy / humidity- and contact-aware transport models. Physical bench: nonliving saline-polymer skin analogue with calibrated heaters, reference thermistor, impedance bridge and ambient humidity chamber. Strong baseline: temperature-only or impedance-only calibrated estimator with identical sample, instrument and parameter-tuning budgets. Primary endpoint: temperature-corrected impedance residual [ohm]. Critical rival: sweat analogue, humidity, self-heating, optical emissivity, skin-phantom thickness or contact-pressure confounding. Noncompensable stop: unbounded temperature rise in phantom, current-source calibration loss, unsafe conductive path, or treating thermal maps as an acupoint signature. Five evidence channels must never be reduced to a flattering fusion score. The falsifiable claim is transferred from one laboratory to another only after physical scale, reference identity, data selection, external event time, software version and valid authorization are declared. The source lineage may motivate a new hypothesis, but the assertion must survive a separate experiment. Physical bench: an inert layered acoustic phantom with ultrasound transducer, embedded reference electrodes and known optical fiducials; no needle placement into persons. Strong baseline: best single independently calibrated ultrasound or electrical localization pipeline under identical acquisition and operator budgets. Primary endpoint: blinded phantom landmark localization error [mm]. Critical rival: speed-of-sound mismatch, probe compression, ultrasound reverberation, gel-shared electrodes and circular landmark registration. The falsifiable claim is transferred from one laboratory to another only after physical scale, reference identity, data selection, external event time, software version and valid authorization are declared. The source lineage may motivate a new hypothesis, but the assertion must survive a separate experiment. F019 — Cross-modal synchronization and calibration Core three-coupling: separate clock domains / external timing-pulse metrology / versioned drift and resampling corrections. Physical bench: three-channel electronic, mechanical and thermal phantom acquisition rig with independently timed trigger and clock-swap board. Strong baseline: independently time-stamped best single sensor and transparent fixed-offset synchronization with identical timing hardware. Primary endpoint: external cross-sensor time skew [ms]. Critical rival: shared clock leakage, interpolation artefacts, dropped events, timer wraparound, asymmetric buffer delay and unreported clock resets. Noncompensable stop: clock identity ambiguity, unbounded timestamp skew, nonrecoverable packet loss, or unqualified cross-device unit conversion. Five evidence channels must never be reduced to a flattering fusion score. A joint model cannot substitute for physical calibration or the best single-sensor comparison. The falsifiable claim is transferred from one laboratory to another only after physical scale, reference identity, data selection, external event time, software version and valid authorization are declared. The source lineage may motivate a new hypothesis, but the assertion must survive a separate experiment. Critical rival: training-test leakage, correlated channels, ill-conditioned observability, phantom batch confounding and confident hallucination of latent biology. Noncompensable stop: unobservable state, failing calibration, out-of-distribution input, unauthorized intervention or transfer of simulated reconstruction to human diagnosis. Five evidence channels must never be reduced to a flattering fusion score. summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement. summary: This version (v3.1.0-2021-2024) contains reproducibility materials for the 2021-2024 National Immunization Survey-Teen analysis of parent-reported clinician recommendation, preventive-care access, and insurance gaps in U.S. adolescent HPV vaccination. The provider-phase sample comprises 66,938 adolescents aged 13-17 years, and multivariable complete-case models comprise 60,338 adolescents. Relative to v3.0.0-2021-2024 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22796335), every statistical analysis script (01, 02, 04, 07, 08) and all 35 aggregate statistical and diagnostic tables are preserved byte-for-byte without refitting any models. This update upgrades script 06_ahp_figures.R, the PDF/SVG vector exports for Figures 1-3 and Supplementary Figure S1, and their companion aggregate figure source-data CSVs to match journal artwork conventions (adding the annual recommendation-stratified up-to-date panel to Figure 1, expanding Figure 2 to display both primary overall and insurance-stratified adjusted probabilities and differences, and adding private-insurance benchmark reference lines to Figure 3). The package includes six scientific R scripts, an optional public CDC downloader, a dependency checker, aggregate analysis and diagnostic tables (including 999 Rao-Wu stratified bootstrap replicates for two-stage inverse-probability complete-case weighting and complete six-category reason reporting), source data and PDF/SVG exports for three main figures and one supplementary figure, software session records, execution-verification files, and SHA-256 checksums. Primary adjusted recommendation-associated differences are 21.7 and 22.5 percentage points for initiation and up-to-date vaccination; IPCW sensitivity differences are 21.2 and 22.1 points. Script 01 reads source files for 2018-2024; script 04 restricts the analysis to 2021-2024 and uses annual provider weights divided by four. Run scripts in the order documented in the README: dependency check, 01, 04 with --skip-ipcw, 07 final 999 8, 08, and 06. summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FAIR-bioHeaders Specification

summary: eglish version)This work presents a three-parameter mechanical-medium framework for the forward derivation of physical constants and characteristic scales within the Four-Forces–Quantum-Induction research program. The central objective is to determine how a minimal set of medium parameters can generate a hierarchy of microscopic and macroscopic physical quantities through a closed forward construction, rather than through post-hoc fitting to target observations. The current formulation includes an absolute-scale solution that no longer requires Newton’s gravitational constant as an external scale-setting calibration. Newton’s constant is instead used as a downstream consistency and round-trip closure test. The framework develops explicit relations among the characteristic medium density, elastic scale, viscosity-related input, characteristic radii, effective gravitational quantities, particle-scale structures, and derived observables. Strict NoAlias and NoDoubleCount rules are applied throughout to prevent numerically similar quantities or multiple readouts of the same physical inventory from being incorrectly identified or counted twice. An independent internal consistency test is provided by two routes to the model’s Hubble-equivalent scale. A global-field calculation and a local curvature or pressure-gradient calculation converge to approximately 67.33789544 km/s/Mpc. This quantity is reported as a model Hubble-equivalent scale. Its exact identification with the standard cosmological expansion rate H0 remains subject to a separate clock-identity condition and is therefore not assumed. The release also incorporates the current charge-conjugate electron-origin structure and the resulting birth-population asymmetry. The frozen current value is 6.117043204146319e-10. This result is treated as a theoretical output of the current model structure and is not presented as a new blind observational test. A strict theory-to-evidence firewall is maintained throughout the project. The workflow is: authority snapshot, declared inputs, forward operator, frozen prediction, external evidence, and statistical or qualitative score. Observational information is not permitted to modify a prediction after the prediction has been frozen. The empirical portfolio is intentionally reported with mixed outcomes. It includes compatible historical cross-checks, the Hubble-equivalent forward result with its explicit clock qualifier, cosmic-age consistency checks, an electron g-2 comparison that currently fails the frozen operator at high experimental precision, ring-laser results that remain retrospective rather than a new blind holdout, and prospective constant-drift predictions reserved for future evaluation. Compatible but non-discriminating tests are distinguished from genuinely discriminating evidence. The accompanying archive contains the English manuscript, validation and evidence status material, selected derivation records, Hubble-equivalent and asymmetry authority snapshots, provenance and reproducibility information, SHA256 manifests, and the sealed v4.43 historical authority package. This Zenodo release should therefore be interpreted as a frozen research record of the current theoretical construction, its absolute-scale closure, its derived cross-scale relations, and its explicitly classified empirical status. It is not a claim that every external observable has been successfully reproduced. Failed, conditional, prospective, and not-yet-opened evidence channels are retained explicitly as part of the scientific record.     预印本 — 未经同行评审。

summary: Modern AI assistants, agents, and decision-support systems increasingly rely on information beyond model parameters by retrieving documents, accessing memory, invoking tools, and combining external evidence. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is one prominent realization of this broader information-grounding paradigm. Yet external grounding does not by itself ensure trustworthiness. Systems can still fail under incomplete, noisy, conflicting, or misleading evidence, and these failures become harder to diagnose as retrieval, reasoning, memory, tool use, and generation interact. Existing evaluation frameworks measure important aspects of system quality, but do not necessarily ensure deliberate coverage of the conditions most likely to expose system vulnerabilities. We introduce PRISM as a methodology for systematic stress testing of retrieval-grounded AI through controlled synthetic data generation. Rather than treating evaluation data as a static benchmark, PRISM constructs and validates document and question-answer pairs designed to reproduce deployment-relevant failure conditions. Its 25 evaluation instruments are organized across ten diversity dimensions and eight thematic clusters, covering conditions such as fragmented or noisy evidence, lexical and semantic mismatch, unanswerable queries, and adversarial or epistemically unreliable content. Because these conditions are generated synthetically, they can reproduce relevant document and evidence characteristics without requiring access to proprietary or sensitive operational data. Stress conditions are also linked to concrete system choices to support targeted diagnosis. PRISM is expected to provide reproducible and traceable evaluation artifacts that help reveal vulnerabilities before deployment and distinguish failures originating from retrieval, evidence selection, generation, or abstention. Automated construction and validation are also intended to reduce the manual effort associated with human-curated evaluation sets while preserving the control, coverage, and consistency needed for systematic evaluation. More broadly, PRISM reframes evaluation as not only a measurement problem but also an experimental-design problem. By complementing existing metrics, human evaluation, observability, and post-deployment monitoring, it contributes toward more systematic pre-deployment assessment of increasingly agentic, retrieval-grounded AI systems.
title: Toward Trustworthy Retrieval-Grounded AI through Synthetic Stress Testing

Automated construction and validation are also intended to reduce the manual effort associated with human-curated evaluation sets while preserving the control, coverage, and consistency needed for systematic evaluation. More broadly, PRISM reframes evaluation as not only a measurement problem but also an experimental-design problem. By complementing existing metrics, human evaluation, observability, and post-deployment monitoring, it contributes toward more systematic pre-deployment assessment of increasingly agentic, retrieval-grounded AI systems.
title: Toward Trustworthy Retrieval-Grounded AI through Synthetic Stress Testing

summary: SideCow-VSS is a side-view dairy cow video semantic segmentation dataset developed to support computer vision research in precision livestock farming. The original study describes 921 five-second video clips with dense pixel-level annotations, sampled at 10 frames per second under real dairy farm conditions. The annotations were generated using a semi-automated pipeline involving YOLOv11, SAM2, and manual verification. This version (v1.0.0) provides the currently available JPEG frames and PNG segmentation annotation files, organized into the original training, validation, and testing splits. The release contains 46,024 JPEG files and 46,024 PNG files, distributed as follows: Training: 32,177 JPEG files and 32,177 PNG files. Validation: 6,897 JPEG files and 6,897 PNG files. Testing: 6,950 JPEG files and 6,950 PNG files. The dataset supports semantic segmentation of dairy cows and background regions. The original data partitions and available files are preserved without reconstructing missing frames. For details of dataset construction, annotation methodology, and benchmarking, please refer to the associated publication: Yao, L., Liu, J., Hong, W., Kong, F., Fan, Z., Lei, L., & Li, X. (2025). SideCow-VSS: A Video Semantic Segmentation Dataset and Benchmark for Intelligent Monitoring of Dairy Cows Health in Smart Ranch Environments. Veterinary Sciences , 12(11), 1104. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/vetsci12111104
title: SideCow-VSS: A Side-View Dairy Cow Video Semantic Segmentation Dataset

summary: Configuration-driven Python pipeline (code and locked analysis plan) for the study 'Survey-design-calibrated independence tests reduce adjustment-set validity in PC-based causal discovery'. It implements design-corrected conditional-independence tests (Rao-Scott, design t test), PC-stable with temporal tiers, seven confounder-selection strategies, cross-fitted AIPW with design-based standard errors, and a simulation benchmark mimicking the 2017 Indonesia Demographic and Health Survey. IDHS microdata are not included and must be requested from The DHS Program. Release v1.1 added the deviation log (CATATAN_DEVIASI.md) and the verification scripts and reports in verifikasi/. Release v1.3 adds the verification material for the reproducibility manuscript (verifikasi/naskah3/revisi5/): an AST-based configuration-import checker run over the git history, controlled fault injection, a BLAS thread test, bootstrap seeding schemes, a 2x2 code x configuration benchmark design with Monte Carlo intervals, and OpenTimestamps proofs for two analysis-plan manifests. The application modules causal.py, baseline.py and sol_dag.py now seed the random stream per analysis (deviation log section 8). Release v1.4 adds verification material requested in the review of the reproducibility manuscript (verifikasi/naskah3/revisi6/): detection limits of the import checker on 11 stale-import variants compared with Import Linter and a runtime guard, fault injection derived from an external configuration-error taxonomy (Yin et al., SOSP 2011), Holm correction for the 2x2 design, ULP-based floating-point differences, and an independent check of the OpenTimestamps block attestations. Import Linter is listed separately in requirements-verifikasi.txt so that the locked analysis environment is unchanged.
title: Kausal IDHS: design-based causal graph discovery and confounder selection for complex survey data

summary: Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly operating over longer horizons with diminishing human oversight, raising the risk of loss of control: systems acting beyond effective human control with potentially irreversible consequences. Because such failures may become observable only after containment is difficult, they must be assessed prospectively. We introduce a behavioural framework that decomposes loss-of-control risk into three factors: misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion. We operationalise these factors through 13 measurable aspects and 29 evaluation tasks, whose scores are combined into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score. Across 13 frontier models, the LoC score shows strong prospective validity, correlating with failure rates in contained long-horizon risk scenarios (Pearson r = 0.84). Risk varies systematically across models and cannot be explained by capability alone. We further show that the framework can guide targeted mitigations: fine-tuning and monitoring directed at diagnosed vulnerabilities reduce failure rates while largely preserving general performance. These results provide a practical basis for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risk before it materialises.
title: A Behavioural Framework for Predicting and Understanding Loss of Control in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Systems

summary: Tools that claim to detect emerging research topics are rarely judged on their own lists. Our main contribution is a protocol that makes such judgement possible. A bet freezes four things before its verdict can be known: the date of the photograph, the population of candidates, the verdict rule, and the comparison with chance drawn among the same candidates. The list has a fixed length, is read on two axes (champions and failures) against a computed ceiling, and is sealed by cryptographic fingerprint; sealing proves that a list existed at a date, not that it is right. A topic is a champion if its yearly volume of records triples within three years and reaches 100, a failure if it falls by 30%. We apply the protocol to one detector on PubMed/MEDLINE, in three separate blocks. On a retrospective benchmark (2017-2022), chance among the candidates yields 26.7 champions and 15.1 failures out of 120 slots; the detector yields 85 and 3, and under nine pre-registered variants of the verdict rule its champions stay between 2.5 and 5.0 times chance, with no more failures. The detector was developed with these verdicts known, and its specification is not published. Prospective validation rests on six sealed bets, judged in early 2029 and early 2030; only bets 5 and 6 test exactly the instrument of the benchmark. A secondary, exploratory study applies the same judge to eight research funders: under exact name matching, which may disadvantage grant texts, the detector's lists are more concentrated in future champions than the twenty topics named in the most grants of each funder (70.8% against 20.8% to 35.8%, chance 22.3%). We document data defects, negative results and the limits of each comparison.
title: Sealed bets on emerging research topics: a protocol for judging early detection, applied to a detector and to eight research funders

summary: Capability benchmarks measure what large language models can do, but not whether their recommendations remain appropriate as decision conditions change. This paper proposes a trajectory-based measurement framework and prospective validation protocol for artificial wisdom, defined behaviorally as context-sensitive regulation of judgment. Versioned reference specifications determine admissible responses and transition materiality before evaluation. Seven stage-level criteria assess judgment under current conditions, while two transition components assess material-update adequacy and commitment-preserving stability. Stability requires prior adequacy; switching within registered commitment classes is permitted, and persistent error earns no stability credit. A nine-component profile is primary, with a secondary bottleneck score and separate critical-failure reporting. Three simplified simulations examine precision, bottleneck estimation, and sensitivity to model-family count. A single-criterion simulation met its precision criteria at 24 scenarios per domain. Near a bottleneck tie, the estimated minimum had a downward bias of 0.55 points at that size. A simplified incremental-prediction simulation detected a Brier improvement of 0.027 with probabilities of .508 and .742 using eight and twelve families, respectively; it does not establish power for the operational protocol. An exploratory predecessor-rubric study comprising 71 evaluation records illustrates aggregation sensitivity but does not validate the proposed instrument. The twelve-family target remains provisional pending feasibility assessment and calibration of the complete analysis. Whether the profile predicts independent decision outcomes beyond capability remains an open empirical question.
title: Evaluating Artificial Wisdom (AW): A Trajectory-Based Framework for Context-Sensitive Decision Regulation

summary: Objective: Choosing between noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS) and invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for acute respiratory failure is a time-sensitive decision. Although guidelines provide population-level guidance, it remains unclear who benefits more from NIRS than IMV. The standard outcome, ventilator-free days at 28 days (VFD-28), scores death and prolonged ventilation equally, and current estimators do not distinguish between them. We developed and validated a censoring-aware Digital Twin framework for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support (DINIRS) to estimate individualized treatment effects (ITEs) that capture both mortality and ventilation duration. Materials and Methods: We emulated a target trial in 5,336 MIMIC-IV patients and trained DINIRS on 23 baseline clinical variables measured during the first 24 ICU hours. A transformer encoder with a survival attention gate decomposed VFD-28 into survival probability and conditional ventilation duration. A cross-fitted, doubly robust learner estimated ITEs. We externally validated DINIRS in 2,540 patients from the multi-site eICU-CRD dataset without retraining. Results: The DINIRS policy achieved a mean benefit of 2.07 ventilator-free days per patient (207 per 100 patients) compared with observed practice. Predicted NIRS benefit was higher among patients with less organ dysfunction (88.4% versus 49.0%) and persisted across hypoxemia severity. External validation reproduced this pattern. Discussion: The NIRS benefit stemmed from shorter ventilation among survivors rather than from reduced mortality, indicating that avoiding intubation-associated complications was the primary mechanism. Conclusion: Prospective validation is needed before these estimates inform treatment decisions. The decomposition framework can be extended beyond respiratory support to any zero-inflated composite outcome.
title: A Digital Twin for Individualized Treatment Effects of Non-Invasive Respiratory Support Strategies (DINIRS)

summary: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with increased risks of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. Recent ECG foundation models offer transferable representations for automated AF detection. However, their relative effectiveness remains unclear because existing studies use different datasets, preprocessing procedures, classifiers, and validation protocols. This study presents FOUND-AF, a unified, leakage-controlled, and deployment-oriented benchmarking framework that evaluates the quality of pretrained ECG representations under identical experimental conditions. Nine publicly available foundation models from five families, including HuBERT-ECG, CLEF, ST-MEM, ECG-JEPA, and ECGFounder, were evaluated across four heterogeneous ECG datasets, namely AFDB, CinC2017, CPSC2021, and LTAFDB. All models were used as frozen feature extractors with standardized preprocessing, model-native resampling, a fixed XGBoost classifier, and recording-level grouped cross-validation. The evaluation included classification metrics, receiver operating characteristic analysis, paired recording-level bootstrap comparisons with Holm correction, embedding-space visualization, and computational efficiency profiling. The ECGFounder model consistently achieved the strongest overall performance across datasets while offering a favorable trade-off between accuracy, model size, inference time, and memory usage. FOUND-AF therefore provides a reproducible framework for selecting ECG foundation models and demonstrates that compact, clinically pretrained encoders can support robust and computationally efficient AF detection across heterogeneous acquisition settings.
title: FOUND-AF: Benchmarking ECG Foundation Models for Atrial Fibrillation Detection

summary: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.
title: Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks

summary: Tuning of gate-defined semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) is a major bottleneck for scaling spin qubit technologies. We present a deep learning (DL) driven, semantic-segmentation pipeline that performs charge auto-tuning by locating transition lines in full charge stability diagrams (CSDs) and returns gate voltage targets for the single charge regime. We assemble and manually annotate a large, heterogeneous dataset of 1015 experimental CSDs measured from silicon QD devices, spanning nine design geometries, multiple wafers, and fabrication runs. A U-Net style convolutional neural network (CNN) with a MobileNetV2 encoder is trained and validated through five-fold group cross validation. Our model achieves an overall offline tuning success of 80.0% in locating the single-charge regime, with peak performance exceeding 88% for some designs. We analyze dominant failure modes and propose targeted mitigations. Finally, wide-range diagram segmentation also naturally enables scalable physic-based feature extraction that can feed back to fabrication and design workflows and outline a roadmap for real-time integration in a cryogenic wafer prober. summary: Camera images are ubiquitous in machine learning research. They also play a central role in the delivery of important services spanning medicine and environmental surveying. However, the application of machine learning models in these domains has been limited because of robustness concerns. A primary failure mode are performance drops due to differences between the training and deployment data. While there are methods to prospectively validate the robustness of machine learning models to such dataset drifts, existing approaches do not account for explicit models of the primary object of interest: the data. This limits our ability to study and understand the relationship between data generation and downstream machine learning model performance in a physically accurate manner. In this study, we demonstrate how to overcome this limitation by pairing traditional machine learning with physical optics to obtain explicit and differentiable data models. We demonstrate how such data models can be constructed for image data and used to control downstream machine learning model performance related to dataset drift. The findings are distilled into three applications. First, drift synthesis enables the controlled generation of physically faithful drift test cases to power model selection and targeted generalization. Second, the gradient connection between machine learning task model and data model allows advanced, precise tolerancing of task model sensitivity to changes in the data generation. These drift forensics can be used to precisely specify the acceptable data environments in which a task model may be run. Third, drift optimization opens up the possibility to create drifts that can help the task model learn better faster, effectively optimizing the data generating process itself. A guide to access the open code and datasets is available at https://github.com/aiaudit-org/raw2logit.
title: Data Models for Dataset Drift Controls in Machine Learning With Optical Images

summary: Acoustic indices are widely used as rapid proxies for biodiversity, but they summarise the distribution of sound energy rather than the species producing it and often track richness poorly. We revise and test an Acoustic Biodiversity Index (ABI) built from species-level detections. Its primary form, ABI_E, is Shannon diversity of detections normalised by the regional species pool expected at the site and season (H / ln S_ref); temporal stability T is reported as a separate component. We first benchmarked four classifiers on a strongly labelled tropical dataset (1,216 calls, 24 classes) with recording-grouped cross-validation. BirdNET embeddings + logistic regression performed best (macro-F1 0.750 +/- 0.029), and random frame-level splits inflated accuracy from 0.41 to 0.70. We then applied BirdNET v2.4 with a location and season filter to recordings from a riverine savanna in the Zambezi Valley, Zimbabwe, and from three habitats at Emirates Park Zoo and Resort, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. A stricter post-hoc location filter removed 517 high-confidence detections of 9 implausible species, all at the zoo. After diel-matched rarefaction to equal effort (6 h), the savanna site held 21 species (Hill number 1D = 9.83; ABI_E = 0.38) against 1.3-13 species (ABI_E = 0.03-0.21) at the zoo sites. Across 149 recorded hours, ABI_E correlated strongly with richness (Spearman rho = 0.93), whereas six standard indices did not (best: ACI, rho = 0.48). The stability term was lower at the savanna site (0.39) than at the zoo (0.65-0.67), showing that it penalises the natural diel cycle of bird activity. Species-level indices with explicit false-positive control, a declared regional reference pool and effort standardisation provide a more interpretable biodiversity indicator than energy-based acoustic indices.
title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo

summary: The study examines the physiological adaptation of boxers to mid-altitude conditions (1,800‒2,200 m above sea level) and substantiates the need to individualize training loads based on functional markers: blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), heart rate (HR), lactate levels, and maximum oxygen consumption (VO2). The article presents the results of a pedagogical experiment involving 24 qualified boxers (CMS and MS), divided into control and experimental groups. The experimental methodology included real-time monitoring of functional markers and real-time adjustment of the weekly microcycle. Following a 4-week high-altitude training camp, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase in VO2 by 6.8%, hemoglobin concentration by 4.3%, and an improvement in the heart rate recovery index by 34.4% compared to the control group (p<0.05). title: Individualization of Boxing Training Loads in Middle-Altitude Conditions Based on Functional Adaptation Markers.

summary: Core Objective : To construct pure quantum Yang-Mills theory with compact simple gauge group $SU(N)$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space, prove the strict positivity of its mass gap, and reduce the mass-gap problem to a small set of explicit, identified inputs. Factorizes the mass-gap problem into three independent aspects: Existence (forced by reflection positivity and Fekete's lemma), Value (governed by an anomalous dimension), and Positivity (carried by the discrete centre of the gauge group and uniform control of confining flux). summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. summary: We present a systematic study of the quantum phase transition from a Dirac semimetal to an antiferromagnetic Mott insulator in the honeycomb-lattice Hubbard model, using finite-temperature auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) simulations. Given the dynamical critical exponent $z=1$ at criticality, we scale the inverse temperature $β$ with the linear system size $L$, i.e., $βt=L$ (with $t$ as the hopping amplitude), to approach the thermodynamic and zero-temperature limits simultaneously. On the algorithmic front, we generalize the fast Fourier transform in path propagation to multi-sublattice systems and employ the delayed update technique in configuration updates to accelerate the AFQMC simulations. These advances enable us to access unprecedented system sizes of up to $3528$ sites (with $L=42$ and $βt = 42$). We additionally use twist-averaged boundary conditions to reduce the finite-size effects in computed observables. On the physical side, we determine the Dirac quantum criticality via finite-size scaling analysis of the spin correlations and off-diagonal single-particle Green's function, and locate the critical point at $U_c/t=3.731(4)$ with the critical exponents $ν=1.097(7)$, $η_φ=0.72(2)$ and $η_ψ=0.155(6)$. We further corroborate the critical point by examining several relevant quantities, including the quasiparticle weight, Fermi-liquid parameter, charge compressibility, $U$-derivative of double occupancy, and fidelity susceptibility. Our work establishes an independent benchmark for the chiral Heisenberg Gross-Neveu-Yukawa criticality in the honeycomb Hubbard model, offering a complementary perspective to previous ground-state simulations.
title: Finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo study of Dirac quantum criticality: Algorithmic advances and comprehensive analysis

summary: We develop and validate a one-dimensional electron-ion two-fluid model, self-consistently coupled to Maxwell equations, for magnetosonic structures generated by a moving charged source. The model is independently benchmarked against kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to assess its ability to reproduce electrostatic and electromagnetic responses. summary: Supporting code and data for the exploratory ETV4 case study “Sequence and family context shape ETV4 representations in protein language models”. The deposit contains 711 biological/control activation arrays from ESM-2 650M, ESM-2 3B and ProFam, 71 numerical-qualification arrays with receipts, and a versioned repository snapshot containing processed results, input sequences and prompts, fixed readout masks and configurations, analysis and figure-generation code, provenance and supplementary information. A portable NumPy analysis verifies array identities and recomputes both canonical summaries without rerunning the protein models. All saved fields, including 107,102 numerical values, matched in local verification. The study examines dependence of protein representations on sequence and family context; it does not establish regulatory specificity or an allosteric mechanism. Original code is licensed under MIT; original derived data and written materials are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their own terms. The code snapshot filename identifies its Git commit. Development repository: https://github.com/amoyag/etv4-context-representations .

summary: We present the first mechanised formalisation of Romanov's Triplet Logic (TLS) in the Rocq proof assistant. TLS is a combinatorial framework originally motivated by Boolean satisfiability, based on triplet structures and a filter that we call Simple Vertex Intersection (SVI). We formalise the core of TLS, including its translation from 3-CNF, the clearing procedure, and the SVI algorithm. For the well-formed sliding-window fragment, we prove explicit polynomial-time bounds for the filter stages and verify the translation and intersection operations. Our main contribution is a precise correctness boundary: for general formulas, SVI non-emptiness is necessary but not sufficient for satisfiability; for aligned structures, we prove a full bi-implication, extended to systems of structures. We also formalise the grouped-window translation and provide a formal counterexample to its completeness. We introduce VFR (Verified Filter for Romanov's triplet logic), an extracted OCaml prototype that implements a verified decision procedure for the sliding-window fragment and a sound filter for general 3-CNF, with a Python runtime and Docker packaging. Benchmarks corroborate the predicted behaviour, and the complete toolchain is available as a curated Zenodo artifact. The Rocq development comprises over 23,000 lines of code, with 424 proved lemmas and no unproved assumptions.
title: Formal Verification of Romanov's Triplet Logic: A Verified Filter for Sliding-window 3-CNF with Application to Structured Formulas

summary: We present JOR-Bench, a collection of five Japanese-language benchmarks for evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to formulate and solve operations research (OR) problems. Each benchmark is a Japanese translation of an existing English benchmark: IndustryOR, MAMO Complex LP, NL4OPT, OptiBench, and OptMATH, covering 1,319 problems spanning linear programming, mixed-integer programming, non-linear programming, and combinatorial optimization. JOR-Bench is a solver-independent benchmark that can be used with any solver or programming language, and consists of pairs of Japanese problem statements and expected numerical answers. We evaluate seven LLMs, including multilingual general-purpose models and Japanese-specialized models, on both the original English and the new Japanese versions, and compare performance across languages. For the main evaluation, we standardize execution with the Python interface to OR-Tools to make model outputs comparable and reproducible with open-source software. Our results show that OR formulation ability is largely language-neutral for strong multilingual models; the overall average accuracy difference between English and Japanese is only $-0.3$ pp. Yet error analysis reveals subtle cross-lingual differences, including a pragmatic disambiguation failure in some domains that causes models to output decision-variable values instead of the objective value when the prompt is in Japanese.
title: JOR-Bench: Japanese Operations Research Benchmarks for Large Language Models

summary: Mathematical reasoning demands two critical, complementary skills: constructing rigorous proofs for true statements and discovering counterexamples that disprove false ones. However, current AI efforts in mathematics focus almost exclusively on proof construction, often neglecting the equally important task of finding counterexamples. In this paper, we address this gap by fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) to reason about and generate counterexamples. We formalize this task as formal counterexample generation, which requires LLMs not only to propose candidate counterexamples but also to produce formal proofs that can be automatically verified in the Lean 4 theorem prover. To enable effective learning, we introduce a symbolic mutation strategy that constructs candidate counterexample-generation tasks by systematically extracting theorems and removing selected hypotheses. Together with curated datasets, this strategy enables a multi-reward expert iteration framework that substantially enhances both the effectiveness and efficiency of training LLMs for counterexample generation and theorem proving. Experiments on three newly collected benchmarks validate the advantages of our approach, showing that the mutation strategy and training framework yield substantial performance gains.
title: Learning to Disprove: Formal Counterexample Generation with Large Language Models

summary: Hydrogen threatens the structural integrity of metals and thus predicting hydrogen-material interactions is key to unlocking the role of hydrogen in the energy transition. Quantifying the interplay between material deformation and hydrogen diffusion ahead of cracks and other stress concentrators is key to the prediction and prevention of hydrogen-assisted failures. In this work, a generalised theoretical and computational framework is presented that for the first time encompasses: (i) stress-assisted diffusion, (ii) hydrogen trapping due to multiple trap types, rigorously accounting for the rate of creation of dislocation trap sites, (iii) hydrogen transport through dislocations, (iv) equilibrium (Oriani) and non-equilibrium (McNabb-Foster) trapping kinetics, (v) hydrogen-induced softening, and (vi) hydrogen uptake, considering the role of hydrostatic stresses and local electrochemistry. Particular emphasis is placed on the numerical implementation in COMSOL Multiphysics, releasing the relevant models and discussing stability, discretisation and solver details. Each of the elements of the framework is independently benchmarked against results from the literature and implications for the prediction of hydrogen-assisted fractures are discussed. The second part of this work (Part II) shows how these crack tip predictions can be combined with crack growth simulations.
title: A COMSOL framework for predicting hydrogen embrittlement -- Part I: coupled hydrogen transport

summary: We study the performance of sequential contention resolution and matching algorithms on random graphs with vanishing edge probabilities. When the edges of the graph are processed in an adversarially-chosen order, we derive a new OCRS that is $0.382$-selectable, attaining the "independence benchmark" from the literature under the vanishing edge probabilities assumption. Complementary to this positive result, we show that no OCRS can be more than $0.390$-selectable, significantly improving upon the upper bound of $0.428$ from the literature. We also derive negative results that are specialized to bipartite graphs or subfamilies of OCRSs. Meanwhile, when the edges of the graph are processed in a uniformly random order, we show that the simple greedy contention resolution scheme which accepts all active and feasible edges is $1/2$-selectable. This result is tight due to a known upper bound. We then show that when the algorithm can choose the processing order, a slight tweak to the random order---give each vertex a random priority and process edges in lexicographic order---results in a strictly better contention resolution scheme that is $1-\ln(2-1/e)\approx0.510$-selectable. Moreover, we show that this bound is tight over any sequential contention resolution scheme, even one which may adaptively choose the order in which it processes edges. This provides a separation from the $0.544$ upper bound for offline contention resolution implied by the classic result of Karp and Sipser. Our positive results also apply to online matching on $1$-uniform random graphs with vanishing (non-identical) edge probabilities, extending and unifying some results from the random graphs literature.
title: Online Matching and Contention Resolution for Edge Arrivals with Vanishing Probabilities

summary: We introduce an automated, formal, counterexample-based approach to synthesise Barrier Certificates (BC) for the safety verification of continuous and hybrid dynamical models. The approach is underpinned by an inductive framework: this is structured as a sequential loop between a learner, which manipulates a candidate BC structured as a neural network, and a sound verifier, which either certifies the candidate's validity or generates counter-examples to further guide the learner. We compare the approach against state-of-the-art techniques, over polynomial and non-polynomial dynamical models: the outcomes show that we can synthesise sound BCs up to two orders of magnitude faster, with in particular a stark speedup on the verification engine (up to five orders less), whilst needing a far smaller data set (up to three orders less) for the learning part. Beyond improvements over the state of the art, we further challenge the new approach on a hybrid dynamical model and on larger-dimensional models, and showcase the numerical robustness of our algorithms and codebase.
title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models

summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 42 examines why enterprise artificial intelligence strategy is moving beyond the assumption that one general-purpose model should serve every workload. The paper argues that model selection is increasingly an intelligence-allocation decision involving capability, cost, latency, governance, data restrictions, decision authority and measurable business outcomes. As enterprise AI expands across routine classification, specialised extraction, complex reasoning, multimodal production and consequential decisions, different categories of work require different execution approaches. The paper distinguishes model selection, inference tiering, model routing, policy-controlled routing and outcome verification. It proposes that enterprises should first determine whether generative inference is required, define the minimum capability needed, apply mandatory eligibility constraints, select an appropriate execution route, establish escalation conditions and verify whether the completed outcome meets a predetermined business acceptance standard. Six author-developed frameworks structure this operating model. The AI Workload Classification framework divides work into deterministic, routine language, specialised, complex reasoning and consequential-decision categories. The Model Routing Matrix separates mandatory policy constraints from economic and performance preferences. The Capability-Cost Frontier evaluates eligible models against verified acceptance and complete delivery cost. The Model Escalation Ladder defines structured movement from deterministic execution through compact, specialised and frontier intelligence to human authority. Minimum Sufficient Intelligence identifies the least expensive eligible intelligence capable of satisfying the complete business requirement. Cost per Accepted Outcome, or CPAO, measures total attributable workflow delivery cost against completed business outcomes that satisfy defined acceptance standards. The analysis also challenges the assumption that sophisticated routing automatically produces superior economics. Evidence from LLMRouterBench shows strong model complementarity while demonstrating that several routing approaches do not consistently outperform simpler baselines. The paper therefore argues that routing complexity requires evidence of incremental value rather than being treated as an architectural objective in itself. Commercial case studies examine three different intelligence-allocation mechanisms. Sword Health illustrates central gateway control, provider portability, policy enforcement and cost attribution. Forethought demonstrates how specialised deployment, multi-model endpoints and serverless inference affect AI infrastructure economics. gimmefy illustrates multimodel execution across different marketing modalities and provider capabilities. The cases are treated separately because their reported outcomes rely on different commercial baselines and measurement approaches. The paper proposes a 90-day evaluation path based on workload classification, baseline measurement, shadow testing, controlled deployment and an explicit investment decision. Leadership measurement should focus on accepted outcome rate, cost per accepted outcome, realised business value, consequential errors, latency distribution, policy compliance, escalation and rework, and model substitution readiness. The central argument is that enterprise advantage will come from disciplined allocation of intelligence rather than maximising model capability or model count. The appropriate question is which intelligence should handle each workload, under what authority, and at what verified cost of successful execution. summary: Herrero García, José Luis. “La reivindicación marroquí y la soberanía española sobre Ceuta y Melilla.” Boletín CODESEL , vol. 2, no. 11, Oct. 2026, pp. 1–15. ISSN 3045-7750 LEGAL REVIEW The territorial claims advanced by the Kingdom of Morocco concerning Ceuta, Melilla and the remaining Spanish territories in North Africa constitute a particularly complex controversy at the intersection of international public law, historical sovereignty, territorial integrity, decolonisation and European security. Although these claims are frequently presented through the political vocabulary of colonial restitution and national reunification, their historical and legal foundations require examination beyond the geographical proximity of the disputed territories or the nationalist narratives surrounding Morocco's independence. In this extensive historical and juridical study, José Luis Herrero García undertakes a systematic examination of Moroccan territorial revisionism and the legal continuity of Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. His principal argument challenges the doctrine of Greater Morocco by distinguishing premodern religious allegiances, dynastic dominion and military expansion from the legal characteristics of territorial sovereignty under contemporary international law. Through the combined analysis of medieval political formations, historical treaties, constitutional provisions, international judicial reasoning and European institutional practice, the article develops a comprehensive interpretation of the historical and legal circumstances supporting Spain's position. The significance of the study extends beyond the bilateral dispute, raising fundamental questions concerning the construction of historical territorial titles, the stability of international borders and the limitations imposed by international law upon irredentist claims. The analysis begins with the historical development of Moroccan territorial ambitions, tracing the ideological origins of the Greater Morocco doctrine to nationalist movements that emerged during the first half of the twentieth century and acquired particular prominence around Moroccan independence in 1956. Herrero García identifies the influence of Allal el Fassi and the Istiqlal Party in formulating an expansive conception of Moroccan territorial identity that encompassed not only Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish possessions, but also Western Sahara, Mauritania, territories in present-day Algeria and parts of the Sahel. This geographical conception was supported by references to the alleged historical boundaries of successive Islamic dynasties and to the religious and political relationships established between Moroccan rulers and neighbouring populations. The author questions the legitimacy of interpreting such relationships as evidence of an uninterrupted historical sovereignty comparable to that exercised by modern States. This criticism is particularly important because the nationalist reconstruction of medieval territorial boundaries disregards the institutional differences between dynastic empires, tribal confederations and the contemporary territorial State. The study therefore distinguishes the historical existence of political influence from the establishment of an internationally recognisable sovereign title, arguing that the territorial expansion of former ruling dynasties cannot automatically generate legal entitlements for the present Moroccan monarchy. One of the article's most substantial contributions is its detailed reconstruction of the Almoravid, Almohad, Marinid and Saadian political formations. The discussion of the Almoravids emphasises their origins among Saharan Berber communities associated with territories situated in present-day Mauritania, thereby questioning the assumption that their subsequent expansion establishes a uniquely Moroccan historical entitlement. summary: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 43 examines the governance and evidence requirements that arise when artificial intelligence influences consequential business decisions. The paper defines a decision chain of custody as a controlled, verifiable record connecting the information used, systems involved, applicable policies, delegated authority, approvals, execution and preserved evidence behind an AI-influenced decision. Its central operating test is independent reconstruction: an authorised reviewer should be able to determine what happened, which authority permitted the action and how the resulting business state was verified without relying on the original operator's memory. The analysis distinguishes decision custody from related concepts including accuracy, explainability, data lineage, observability and content provenance. It argues that these controls answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable forms of transparency. Content provenance might identify the history of a digital asset, for example, while providing no evidence that a user held authority to approve a payment or that the resulting transaction was correctly executed. The paper proposes eight linked evidence domains for consequential AI-influenced decisions: information received, intelligence used, rules applied, tools invoked, state changed, authority held, outcome approved and evidence preserved. These domains connect through a shared decision identifier and are intended to preserve relationships between initial inputs, policy evaluation, delegated authority, approval, execution and verified outcome. Particular attention is given to the moment of commitment, when an AI-generated recommendation becomes an external or financial business action. The paper argues that approvals must remain linked to the material terms ultimately executed. Changes to amount, recipient, purpose or other material conditions require a defined re-evaluation path rather than reliance on an earlier approval. The paper also addresses delegation across multiple agents and systems, retry behaviour, transaction reconciliation, evidence integrity, retention, human oversight and supplier evidence obligations. It distinguishes reconstruction from reproduction and outcome verification, noting that exact reproduction of stochastic model output is neither always possible nor necessary for reconstructing observable system behaviour. Three cases illustrate different dimensions of the argument. IBM provides company-reported evidence of reduced data-clearance processing time within an integrated governance programme. HSBC demonstrates large-scale financial-crime detection alongside explainable and auditable investigative outputs. AstraZeneca provides published evidence concerning the organisational scope and challenges of ethics-based AI auditing. None of these cases is presented as proof of a complete decision-custody architecture. The paper proposes consequence-based evidence requirements, independent reconstruction tests, explicit stop conditions for missing authority or mandatory evidence, supplier acceptance tests and measurable indicators including reconstruction pass rate, authority coverage, approval match, outcome reconciliation and preservation verification. The chapter concludes that auditability after an AI-influenced decision is becoming as important as intelligence before the decision. Enterprises expanding autonomous authority should first demonstrate that completed consequential decisions can be independently reconstructed from preserved evidence with clear ownership, valid authority and verified outcomes. The eight-domain decision record, consequence-based evidence model, reconstruction tests and associated management controls are author-developed conceptual frameworks informed by established provenance, AI governance, legal and assurance sources. They are not externally validated standards or universal legal requirements.

summary: Data and analysis code: parental care and mate desertion in the European honey buzzard Associated study Rebollo, S., Díaz-Aranda, L. M., Fernández-Pereira, J. M. & Martín-Ávila, J. A. Parental care and mate desertion in raptors: the case of the European honey buzzard, Pernis apivorus. Accepted manuscript, Animal Behaviour (manuscript 25-00749R3). This deposit provides selected processed, pseudonymized analytical datasets and R scripts associated with the study. It is not a fully validated, end-to-end reproduction package for every result in the accepted manuscript; the scope and limitations are documented below. Repository contents `data/processed/feeding_events_anonymized.csv`: chick feeding observations (assisted versus unassisted), with age, chick order and prey category. Prey categories can overlap; do not treat the full file as a single set of independent events. `data/processed/behaviour_by_nest_phase_anonymized.csv`: nest-level male and female behavioural counts or photographic time proxies, by activity and breeding phase. Not all activities have the same measurement unit. `data/processed/accelerometer_summary_anonymized.csv`: available aggregated accelerometer-derived time summaries; these do not replace the underlying time series. `data/processed/TimingOfLastPreyDelivery_anonymized.csv` and `TimingOfParentalDesertion_anonymized.csv`: paired observations for the timing of the last prey delivery and last nest activity. `data/processed/figure1_male_to_nest_distances.csv`: 217 female prey-delivery events, matched to male-to-nest distances in metres, across five pseudonymized nests. Of these, 58/217 (26.7%) fall below the 857.6 m threshold used in the manuscript. `data/summary/`: transcribed counts from Supplementary Table S8, migration-age arrays obtained from earlier R code, and a historical summary of feeding-transition models. `scripts/reproduction/`: R scripts for selected data checks, statistical analyses and figures. `documentation/`: data dictionaries, checks and known issues. `run_all.R`: runs the available reproduction scripts and reports errors; it does not certify equivalence with all published results. Running the scripts Use R with the packages required by the individual scripts, including `ggplot2` and `lme4`. From the extracted repository's root folder run: ```sh Rscript run_all.R ``` To recreate a version of Figure 1 from the deposited distances: ```sh Rscript scripts/reproduction/03_figure1_kde.R ``` Outputs, where generated, are written to `outputs/`. The scripts were assembled from available source materials but have not been validated by a complete run against the final manuscript. Scope and limitations The Figure 1 distance dataset reproduces the reported 26.7% within 857.6 m. However, time-offset summary statistics derived from this dataset differ from those printed in Supplementary Text S1; the original input/filtering should be checked before interpreting this discrepancy. Pearson chi-square calculations from the printed categories in Supplementary Table S8 yield different chi-square statistics from those in the accepted manuscript, although the conclusions about statistical significance remain unchanged. This discrepancy is documented in `documentation/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` and is not silently corrected in the archived data. The provided scripts do not reproduce every interaction test and bootstrap confidence interval reported for feeding-transition models. The complete GPS/accelerometer time series and raw nest-camera photographs are not deposited. Aggregated time-allocation data do not provide a full reproduction of all incubation analyses. The migration permutation script is included for transparency; its tail direction should be checked against the intended hypothesis before interpreting it as a two-sided test. For further detail, see `documentation/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` and `documentation/FIGURE1_SOURCE_STATUS.md`. Sensitive data and citation Precise nest coordinates, ra
